transcript:
This message comes from Brex. If your best finance people are doing expense reports and
chasing receipts, it's time to get BrexAF, agentic finance that eliminates that work before it starts.
Learn more at brex.com/af. This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder. With less than two weeks to go until midterm election day,
President Trump is keeping a busy travel schedule. He said to campaign in South Carolina later today.
He was in North Carolina last night to support Republican Michael Wadley,
his hand-picked Senate candidate to replace outgoing Senator Tom Tillis.
I said, Michael, I'd love you to run for the Senate. I'm the one that got him into this.
I hope it works. I hope it works. Trump was in North Carolina for the second time in as many
months, urging North Carolina Republicans to turn out on election day to keep Wadley's
Democratic challenger, former governor Roy Cooper from winning the seat. Polls show Cooper with
the lead in a Senate race that could help decide the balance of power in the chamber.
The Trump administration will soon roll out a first-of-its-kind federal voucher program
to help families pay for a range of education costs, including private school tuition.
NPR's Corey Turner reports that states have to opt in or out of the program,
and most Democratic governors are still undecided.
Colorado's Jared Polis was the first and remains one of the only Democratic governors to opt his
state into the new voucher program. That's because he says it can also help public school families
pay for things like tutoring after school. It could be for a summer program you otherwise
couldn't afford, really great opportunities for kids.
But Jessica Levin with Education Law Center sees the program as a Trojan horse.
The way to help public school, she says, is to fund them.
It is not to accept a privatization program that throws a few crumbs at public school students.
16 undecided governors and the mayor of Washington, D.C., have until the end of
the year to opt in or out of the voucher program. Corey Turner, NPR News.
Nigeria has confirmed the country's first Ebola case in Abuja, the capital city.
Health officials are saying the current outbreak is now the most geographically
widespread ever, as NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports.
Nigerian health officials confirmed on Tuesday that a woman who'd been receiving
care at a hospital in Abuja tested positive for Ebola. She'd recently arrived in the
city of over two million on an international flight from Uganda, officials say.
Uganda reported 20 Ebola cases early in this year's outbreak, but was declared
Ebola free in late August. It's unclear where the patient got infected.
Health officials in Nigeria have already identified 44 close contacts of the woman
and are monitoring those who may have been exposed. Nigeria's first case comes days
after the virus arrived in Kenya, where nine people have tested positive.
The Democratic Republic of Congo remains the outbreak's epicenter,
reporting over 9,000 cases and 4,600 deaths since May. Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
And this is NPR News. Florida has carried out its 18th execution of the year under
Republican Governor Ron DeSantis. 77-year-old William Reeves was pronounced
dead Tuesday evening after a lethal injection at the Florida State Prison
near Stark. If another execution is carried out as scheduled next month,
Florida will tie the state record it set last year.
Meanwhile, Alabama's governor is sparing the life of a prisoner on death row.
NPR's Debbie Elliott reports a rare commutation of T'Forrest Johnson's
death sentence comes after a long-fought legal campaign that raised doubts about
the evidence used to convict him. T'Forrest Johnson has maintained his
innocence in the 1995 murder of a sheriff's deputy outside Birmingham.
Now Republican Governor Kay Ivey is commuting his death sentence to life in
prison without parole. Ivey, who has overseen 27 executions,
says this is not a determination of innocence, but that there was not enough
direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death.
Current and former officials, including prosecutors and an Alabama Supreme Court
Justice, supported Johnson's appeals for a new trial. His legal team says it's
grateful to the governor for sparing Johnson's life
and will keep fighting to get his conviction overturned.
Debbie Elliott, NPR News. The NFL says security will be heightened for Sunday's
game in Paris between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the New Orleans Saints.
The NFL says the league security team is on the ground and that officials are
working closely with Paris police following the protests that engulfed the
French capital over the weekend. This is NPR News. This message comes
from IXL, a learning platform for helping kids build confidence
and get up to speed fast. One subscription covers math,

Trump administration rolls out federal school voucher program; Colorado's Jared Polis opts in
Nigeria confirms its first Ebola case, a woman in the capital Abuja
Florida executes William Reeves, its 18th execution this year under Governor DeSantis
Alabama Governor Kay Ivey commutes death sentence of T'Forrest Johnson to life without parole
NFL boosts security for Steelers-Saints Paris game after weekend protests in France
